Cold giants typically have extensive systems of moons and rings. Halvard, which carries a stationary storm larger than Tallis, is a cold giant.

variants.description: The world's clouds are organized into distinct light zones and dark belts in shades of tan, cream and brown, with turbulent eddies along their edges.
The world's appearance is dominated by one or more storms larger than terrestrial planets, persisting for years or centuries.
The world's bands are muted and its storms weak, giving it a pale, washed-out appearance.

types.name: Low-density giant
types.description: A low-density giant is a gas giant with an unusually low mean density, its atmosphere extended far beyond what its mass would ordinarily hold. Some low-density giants are young and still contracting after formation; others are being inflated by heating or tidal forces. Most are losing atmosphere to space, and their extended envelopes make them susceptible to disruption.

variants.description: The world's mean density is comparable to that of light foam, its envelope extending to a radius far beyond that of other giants of similar mass.
The world is still contracting after formation and radiates more heat than it receives from its star.

types.name: Helium giant
types.description: A helium giant is a gas giant whose atmosphere is dominated by helium rather than hydrogen. Such worlds are thought to form when a hot giant loses most of its hydrogen to stellar heating over a long period, leaving the heavier helium behind. Without the methane absorption that colors most giants, helium giants appear grey or white.

variants.description: The world's cloud decks are a featureless grey-white, without the colors or banding typical of hydrogen giants.
The world is the depleted remnant of a former hot giant, smaller and denser than it once was.

types.name: Ice giant
types.description: An ice giant is a giant planet composed mostly of water, ammonia and methane above a rocky core, beneath a comparatively thin envelope of hydrogen and helium. Methane in the upper atmosphere absorbs red light and gives ice giants their blue to blue-green color. Ice giants are common in the outer reaches of Basin systems; they have faint ring systems and families of small, icy moons, and their interiors may hold layers of superionic water.

variants.description: Methane absorption gives the world a deep blue color, with occasional dark storms and bright high clouds.
The world is a paler, hazier blue-green, its features softened by a high-altitude haze.
The world's rotation axis lies close to the plane of its orbit, so that each pole spends decades in continuous daylight and then in darkness.

types.name: Mini-Neptune
types.description: A mini-Neptune is a small gaseous planet, between about two and four times the radius of Earth, with a deep atmosphere of hydrogen and helium over a rocky or icy core and no accessible surface. Mini-Neptunes are among the commonest planets in the galaxy and in the Basin. Their atmospheres may conceal oceans of water or supercritical fluid at depth.

variants.description: A high-altitude photochemical haze shrouds the world, obscuring the deeper atmosphere and giving it a featureless appearance.
A deep layer rich in water lies beneath the world's hydrogen envelope, possibly as an ocean of supercritical fluid.

types.name: Dwarf planet
types.description: A dwarf planet is a body massive enough to have been pulled into a rounded shape by its own gravity but too small to have cleared its orbit of other material. Dwarf planets are common in the outer belts of Basin systems and in the belts of some inner systems. The icy examples may hold thin, seasonal atmospheres of nitrogen or methane that freeze onto the surface when the body is far from its star.

variants.description: The world is composed of ice and rock, its surface coated in nitrogen and methane frost that sublimates and refreezes with the seasons.
The world is composed of rock and metal and lies in an inner asteroid belt, cratered and airless.

types.name: Comet
types.description: A comet is a small body of ice, dust and rock. When its orbit carries it close to its star, the ices sublimate, forming a coma around the nucleus and tails of dust and gas that stream away from the star. Comets captured into stable orbits around planets serve as convenient sources of water in systems without ice moons. Halyard's outer systems are crowded with comets, and they supply much of the trailing arm's water and reaction mass.

variants.description: The world is venting jets of gas and dust from its surface, and it carries a coma and developing tail.
The world's surface volatiles are exhausted, and a dark crust of residue seals the ice beneath it.
The world has been captured into a stable orbit around a planet, where it no longer approaches its star closely enough to become active.

types.name: Moonlet
types.description: A moonlet is a small, irregular moon or rock, usually a captured asteroid or a fragment of a larger body. Moonlets lack the gravity to pull themselves into a rounded shape, and their surface gravity is too weak to hold loose material securely. They are convenient anchors for stations, docks and moorings. The port at Sable is built from hulls moored around the largest of its dark moonlets.

variants.description: The world is a captured asteroid in an irregular, often inclined orbit, its composition unrelated to the planet it orbits.
The world orbits at the edge of a ring and its gravity keeps the ring's boundary sharp.
The world's carbon-rich surface reflects almost no light, and it is difficult to see against the sky.

features.description: The world's rotation is locked to the planet it orbits, so that one hemisphere permanently faces its parent and the other faces away. From the near side the parent hangs fixed in the sky, waxing and waning through its phases.

The world follows a markedly elongated orbit, and the light and heat it receives vary considerably between its closest and farthest approaches to its star. Seasons are governed more by distance than by axial tilt and are unequal in length.

The world orbits in the opposite direction to its parent's rotation and to most other bodies in its system. A retrograde orbit usually indicates that the world was captured rather than formed in place.

The world's orbital period stands in an exact whole-number ratio to that of one or more neighbors, so that their alignments repeat on a fixed schedule. The Orrery's nine worlds are bound in a mutual resonance of this kind.

The world forms a binary pair with a body of comparable size, the two orbiting a common center that lies in the space between them. Each is prominent in the other's sky, and both share an orbit around their star.
The world shares its orbit with a much larger body, holding a stable position sixty degrees ahead of or behind it. Debris and smaller bodies often collect in the same region.
The world did not form in its present orbit but was captured from elsewhere, and its composition differs from that of its neighbors.

The world's axis is tilted so far that its poles in turn face directly toward the star. Each hemisphere passes through months of continuous daylight followed by months of darkness, and seasonal extremes are severe.
The world rotates slowly, with a day lasting weeks or longer. Its surface heats strongly through the long day and cools deeply through the long night.
The world rotates rapidly, with a day of only a few hours. It is visibly flattened at the poles, and its weather is organized into narrow, fast-moving bands.

A system of rings encircles the world, composed of ice, rock or dust and divided into bands by gaps and the influence of small moons. The rings are visible across the sky from the world's surface and from its moons.

The world is exposed to intense radiation from its star, a stellar remnant or trapped radiation belts. Unshielded electronics degrade quickly, and surface work requires shielding and close monitoring of exposure.
The world has a strong magnetic field that deflects much of the stellar wind and traps charged particles in belts around it. The belts are hazardous to cross but protect the surface.
Aurorae are frequent and bright in the world's skies, sometimes reaching far from the poles. They are visible on most nights and can disturb communications.
The world is steadily losing atmosphere to space, driven by heating or stellar wind. The escaping gas can be detected around the world and, in extreme cases, seen as a faint tail.
A field of orbital debris surrounds the world, left by impacts, broken moons or wrecked craft. Navigation near the world requires current charts of the field.

A storm larger than many planets persists in the world's atmosphere and has remained in place for years. It dominates the appearance of the world and the weather around it. Halvard's great storm has not moved in twelve years of observation.
Cloud covers the world without a break, and its star is never seen from the surface. Light at ground level is diffuse and shadowless.
The world's atmosphere circles the planet faster than its surface rotates, sustaining strong winds at all latitudes and carrying weather around the globe in a matter of days.
Dust storms recur on the world, raising fine particles that cover regions or, at times, the entire planet for weeks. Visibility and solar power fall sharply while they last.
Rain on the world is acidic and attacks exposed metal, stone and organic material. Structures and equipment require protective coatings or regular replacement.
Lightning strikes the world at many times the rate of temperate planets, and electrical activity in its storms is a hazard to aircraft and unshielded equipment.
A persistent haze, photochemical or volcanic in origin, hangs in the world's atmosphere. It colors the sky, softens the light at the surface and limits visibility at long range.
Cold, dense winds pour off the world's high ice and plateaus and down into its lowlands, reaching great strength where valleys channel them.

Tidal flexing by the world's parent or a close companion heats its interior. The heat drives volcanism or keeps subsurface liquid from freezing, and the world is geologically more active than its size would suggest.
Volcanoes on the world are active, and eruptions occur somewhere on its surface every year. Fresh lava fields, ash deposits and volcanic gases are features of the landscape.
Volcanoes on the world erupt water, ammonia or methane rather than molten rock, building domes and flows of ice and sometimes venting material into space.
Geysers erupt from the world's surface, venting water or other volatiles in jets that may rise far above the ground. They are concentrated along zones of geological stress or heat.
A body of liquid water lies beneath the world's surface, insulated by rock or ice. Its depth and extent are known only approximately, and it may host life of its own.
A large moon or close parent raises tides of many meters on the world, flooding and exposing broad areas of coast twice in each cycle and driving strong currents through narrow channels.
A single impact basin hundreds of kilometers across dominates one hemisphere of the world, its rim forming a ring of mountains and its floor a broad, low plain.
A canyon system on a continental scale cuts across the world, many times deeper and longer than the largest canyons on settled Union worlds.
Strong earthquakes are frequent on the world, and construction must be designed to withstand them. Fault lines and fresh scarps mark its surface.
Extensive natural cave systems run beneath the world's surface, offering shelter from its climate and radiation and providing access to its interior.
Surface gravity on the world is well below Union standard. Long residence weakens bone and muscle, but launches to orbit are cheap and heavy loads are easily moved.
Areas of the world's surface have been fused into glass by an extreme heating event. The glass is flat, smooth and nearly featureless, cracked into plates by cooling.
The world has an indigenous biosphere. Native life may be simple or complex, but it predates human arrival and is subject to the Charter's native-life protections.
Native life on the world is limited to microorganisms. There are no native plants or animals, but microbial mats and films may cover large areas and alter the chemistry of air and water.

The world supports native animals large enough to threaten a frame. Predators of this size make the open country dangerous and require settlements to be defended. Verdance's predators are the standard example.
Native life on the world poses a serious hazard to settlers through pathogens, toxins, parasites or aggressive predators. Settlement requires medical precautions and perimeter defense.
Native organisms on the world construct large structures from stone, soil or their own secretions. On Cairn, colonial organisms build stone structures several meters high that are observed to move.
Native life on the world is under review for possible sapience under the Charter's native-life protections. A finding of sapience would void claims on the world and restrict access to it.

Absent machinery buried kilometers beneath the world's surface regulates its air and climate. The structures were discovered by survey and are spaced in a pattern that has not been explained. All of the Basin's garden worlds appear to have them.

The Absent machinery regulating the world's climate is failing. Parts of it have stopped entirely while others run erratically, and the world's winters, storms and coastal surges grow worse each year. Orison is the Basin's example.

Absent machinery warms the world from outside its natural energy budget, keeping water liquid where it would otherwise freeze. Nobody has switched one off or explained how it works. The rogue worlds of the Hollows are warmed in this way.
Structures built by the Absent stand on or near the world: towers, platforms, shipyards or constructions of no recognizable purpose. Their age and function are unknown.
A repeating transmission of Absent origin is received from the world or its vicinity at a fixed interval. Its content has not been deciphered, and its source has not been located.
Active Absent machines defend the world's deep workings and attack anyone who digs too close, usually below about four hundred meters. Mining crews treat the depth as a boundary.
Lattice occurs on the world in seams through the rock, much as quartz does, and is mined by seam crews. The work is well paid and dangerous.
Lattice coats parts of the world's surface as thin crusts that appear to have been deposited from outside. The crusts are easy to strip and slow to replace.
Fine grains of lattice are suspended in the world's air, ice or rings, enormous in total quantity but slow to gather in useful amounts.
The world's rings are composed largely of lattice, among the purest deposits known. Choir, in the Shoals, is the example; the local lane to it drifts so fast that no route holds for long.
The remains of a failed or evacuated settlement stand on the world, with structures, equipment and records left in place by those who departed.
The world is under quarantine, closed to landing by order of the Survey Office or another authority. The quarantine is enforced unevenly, and unauthorized landings occur.
The world is the site of recent or continuing fighting. Wrecked frames, fortifications, craters and unexploded ordnance mark the contested ground.
Wrecked ships, frames or structures lie on the world's surface or in its orbit, the remains of accidents, battles or abandoned operations, and are worked by salvagers.
